title: Predicting the unpredictable: Can mathematics teachers learn to anticipate student errors? 2026, 5.15.26
author: Colin Foster and Aidan Stannard
source: Centre for Mathematical Cognition Blog, Loughborough University (blog.lboro.ac.uk), May 11,
summary: Foster and Stannard investigate a specific slice of Lee Shulman's Pedagogical Content Knowledge -- Knowledge of Content and Students -- asking how accurately secondary maths teachers can predict the exact distribution of errors a class will make on a diagnostic multiple-choice question, and whether that predictive skill improves with practice. Working with seven secondary maths teachers across 37 sessions using Craig Barton's Diagnostic Questions website, where every incorrect answer option is engineered to expose a specific misconception, teachers had to predict what percentage of a large real student dataset would choose each option. The task is harder than simply knowing common misconceptions in the abstract: it requires deconstructing each distractor's underlying reasoning and estimating its real-world prevalence. The headline finding is that teachers are both good at this and improve rapidly -- the sharpest gains occurred within the first three practice sessions, with a mean per-session improvement effect size (Cohen's d) of 0.606, driven by the immediate feedback of seeing actual student data against their predictions. The authors argue this points to a practical, low-cost professional development activity: departments spending 10 minutes in a weekly meeting predicting a diagnostic question's answer distribution before revealing the real data. They frame accurate error-anticipation as a direct lever on instructional quality -- teachers who can predict errors design more targeted explanations, select examples that pre-empt specific misconceptions, and pivot mid-lesson with pre-planned responses when a predicted error actually surfaces.
points: The study isolates a precise, measurable skill within Pedagogical Content Knowledge -- predicting the exact percentage distribution of student errors on diagnostic questions, not just knowing common misconceptions exist in general.

Across 37 sessions with seven teachers, predictive accuracy improved with a mean per-session Cohen's d of 0.606, with the sharpest gains occurring in just the first three sessions -- suggesting the skill is fast to build, not a years-long tacit-knowledge accumulation.

The mechanism driving improvement is immediate feedback: teachers' predictions were repeatedly checked against real student response data from Craig Barton's Diagnostic Questions platform, recalibrating their mental model of student thinking each time.

The authors translate the finding into a concrete, low-cost PD design -- a maths department spending 10 minutes of a weekly meeting individually predicting a diagnostic question's answer distribution, then comparing against the real data together.
quotes: The ability to accurately anticipate the errors that are most likely to arise is a teacher super-power, but how good are mathematics teachers at this? And is it something that can be improved through deliberate practice?
Diagnostic questions do not contain haphazard distractors (incorrect options). Instead, every incorrect option is designed to reveal a specific identifiable error or misconception.

This task requires the teacher to do far more than merely identify the correct mathematical answer. They must deconstruct each distractor and understand the particular reasoning that might lead a student to choose one option over another.
We found that our teachers were very good at this and got much better remarkably quickly.

The mean improvement across a single session had a Cohen’s d effect size of 0.606. This suggests that the simple act of repeatedly engaging in this specific predictive task, coupled with the immediate feedback of seeing the actual student data, rapidly hones a teacher’s diagnostic intuition.

A mathematics department could dedicate 10 min of their weekly meetings to looking at a diagnostic question, making individual predictions about the distribution of student answers, and then discussing the actual data.
